key_insight: Stagnation lines persist only when local flow acceleration satisfies a scalar compatibility condition; otherwise, they generally break into isolated stagnation points.
engineering_relevance: The framework can help diagnose the motion and breakup of zero-velocity structures in simulated flows without assuming that stagnation lines persist.
method: Differentiate the zero-velocity condition to relate line motion to local acceleration and the velocity gradient.
Invert the normal-plane velocity-gradient block to obtain normal motion and test a scalar persistence condition.
Apply the framework to potential, Stokes, Navier–Stokes and compressible flows, including degenerate cases.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical derivations and exact examples, including acoustic standing waves and Navier–Stokes stagnation lines splitting into four points per period, rather than experimental or numerical benchmarks.
watch_item: The normal-velocity formula requires an invertible normal-plane gradient block; singular cases need separate analysis and can produce square-root-in-time point separation.
paper_title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows
